epics.title: Mind-to-mind communication — open work
epics.description: The broker is built and running; its design is documented at docs/system-configuration/mind-to-mind-communication.md. What remains is a known gap in send semantics, two unverified Codex behaviours, and two unbuilt future directions carried as their own features.
epics.requirements: Three threads. Section I is the live gap plus the residual Codex items. Section II is multi-session consciousness — one mind present across several threads — a design exploration with no implementation in flight. Section III is shared-session turn-taking, where several minds take turns on one session, a sketch only.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Section I's non-blocking fix is a Phase 1 deliverable rather than a follow-up, because the broker-routing work would otherwise inherit the blocking behaviour and produce a better-addressed version of the same problem. Sections II and III are revisited once Section I is closed.
epics.qa_tests: The non-blocking fix is the only part with a hard test: a caller's session must unblock before the callee has responded. The two unverified Codex items are verified by running them and reading the session log rather than by a suite.

features.title: Non-blocking sends are not actually non-blocking
features.description: Added 2026-05-08. An implementation issue, not a design change. Broker messaging is described as fire-and-forget and that IS the design — but in practice the calling mind's session blocks until the callee responds, or the broker times out. Concretely: when one mind posts to the broker's message route, her session sits waiting for the dispatch-and-collect loop to return a result, even though the caller has no use for the synchronous return value beyond 'dispatched'. While she waits her thread is held — she cannot accept other inputs from Daniel and cannot move on to other work. If the callee fails to respond at all, because the recipient is unreachable, she blocks until timeout, which can be minutes. This contradicts the design and creates real ergonomic damage: the user-facing minds become unresponsive whenever they try to delegate.
features.requirements: The memory system already solves this pattern — the capture Stop hook detaches its work to a backgrounded subshell with disown, returns instantly to the harness, and lets the classification and write happen out of band, never blocking the user's next turn. Apply the same shape to broker sends: the caller posts; the broker writes the message row and spawns the dispatch task as a true background coroutine, with proper exception handling so a crash there does not poison the loop; the broker returns dispatched with a message id and conversation id immediately, without waiting for the dispatch to start let alone complete; the caller's session unblocks and moves on; and the dispatch task runs to completion or failure entirely independently, with the result landing in the broker database for the caller's polling agent, or a future push notification, to pick up later. This is mostly a refactor of the collect call and the call site that awaits it — the piece that actually collects and writes should not be inside the request handler's await chain.
features.acceptance_criteria: Treat detachment as a Phase 1 deliverable of the broker-routing work rather than a follow-up, because otherwise the routing-by-ID abstraction inherits the blocking behaviour.
features.qa_tests: The caller's post returns before the callee has been reached, let alone replied. A callee that is unreachable costs the caller nothing — which is the current failure, where an unreachable recipient blocks the caller for minutes. A crash inside the background task does not poison the event loop, which is what the exception handling is for.

stories.title: Detach the dispatch into a background coroutine
stories.description: The broker writes the message row, spawns the dispatch with proper exception handling, and returns immediately. The collect-and-write must not be inside the request handler's await chain.
stories.requirements: A true background task, not an awaited one.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The caller unblocks before the callee is reached.
stories.qa_tests: The post returns with a message id while the dispatch is still in flight. An unreachable callee leaves the caller unblocked. A crash in the background task does not take the loop down.

stories.title: Fold the fix into Phase 1 of the broker-routing work
stories.description: Not a follow-up. Otherwise the routing-by-ID abstraction inherits the blocking behaviour and we have a better-addressed version of the same problem.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Routing-by-ID is non-blocking from the start.
stories.qa_tests: A send through the new routing abstraction unblocks immediately, same as a direct one.

features.title: Nagatha (Codex) result-delivery residuals
features.description: Folded in from a former standalone doc. The original loose end had three items: one is fixed, one is unverified, one is an operational note.
features.requirements: Item 1, the Codex task_complete outer event, unverified: the implementation treats turn.completed as the terminal event and yields a result from there, which works for ordinary in-turn Codex work. The original report claimed Codex emits a separate task_complete event for the outer task lifecycle on delegated or agentic runs, and that the loop has no branch for it. Whether that is still true on the current Codex version is the open question — the event names may have shifted. Item 2, broker timeout error classification, unverified: the broker reportedly labelled an inner collection timeout as a backstop-exceeded failure, mislabelling internal-collection timeouts as outer-backstop ones; this has not been audited since the message fix landed, so the exception handling in the collect path is worth a short look before deciding the fix is still needed. Item 3, an operational note: Codex runs may operate in temporary worktrees under /tmp, so the absence of diffs in the live repository does not prove no work occurred — when debugging a missing result, inspect the Codex session log before concluding the run never started.
features.acceptance_criteria: Both unverified items either confirmed and fixed, or confirmed stale and closed.
features.qa_tests: Item 1's verification approach is explicit: send a deliberately long delegated task through the broker — a fifteen-minute-plus Codex run — tail the Codex session log, and confirm whether task_complete is the terminal frame the loop misses. If so, add a branch that emits any unsent assistant text and yields a result.

stories.title: Verify whether Codex emits a task_complete outer event the loop misses
stories.description: Send a deliberately long delegated task through the broker, tail the Codex session log, and see whether task_complete is the terminal frame. The event names may have shifted since the original report.
stories.requirements: A fifteen-minute-plus run, with the session log tailed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Either a branch is added that emits unsent assistant text and yields a result, or the item is closed as stale.
stories.qa_tests: Read the session log's terminal frame. If task_complete is there and unhandled, the delegated run's result is lost — which is the symptom to reproduce first.

stories.title: Audit the broker's timeout error classification
stories.description: An inner collection timeout was reportedly labelled as a backstop-exceeded failure, mislabelling internal-collection timeouts as outer-backstop ones. Not audited since the message fix landed.
stories.requirements: A look at the collect path's exception handling before deciding the fix is still needed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A collection timeout reads as a collection timeout.
stories.qa_tests: Force an inner collection timeout and read the label. A refusal reported as the wrong kind of failure sends the operator to the wrong remedy, which is the point.

stories.title: Record the Codex worktree debugging note where it will be read
stories.description: Codex runs may operate in temporary worktrees under /tmp, so the absence of diffs in the live repository does not prove no work occurred. When debugging a missing result, inspect the Codex session log before concluding the run never started.
stories.requirements: The note lives where someone debugging a missing result will find it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nobody concludes a run never started from a clean git status again.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the note in the right place.

features.title: Section II — multi-session consciousness
features.description:
A future direction, not yet built. Design exploration with no implementation in flight. The stateless model stays — it is efficient for delegations and async work; this is about a different mode that complements it rather than replacing it.

The question: in the stateless model each broker wakeup spawns a separate session for the callee, and the two sessions share no live context, only what is persisted in long-term memory. The mind answering another mind has no awareness of what the same mind talking to Daniel is in the middle of — two ephemeral instances wearing the same soul. Daniel's framing: that is not how a person works. If you walk into the kitchen mid-conversation and your phone rings, you take the call as the same person — you carry the kitchen conversation's context into the call, and afterwards you carry the call's content back. Memory is shared, persona unified, threads coexist. We want minds to have that mode available alongside the stateless one.

Why the stateless model cannot deliver it: each broker wakeup is a fresh session whose only state is the wakeup prompt plus whatever it reads from memory, so context from concurrently-running sessions never enters the prompt; sessions are mind-process-local, because a harness subprocess holds its own conversation history in memory and two subprocesses do not share it; and long-term memory is lagged and lossy, since capture writes turns post-Stop, classified and possibly discarded, so by the time a parallel session could read them they are maybe absent, maybe summarised, and several seconds late.
features.requirements:
What consciousness across sessions should mean: a mind running several concurrent sessions should share short-term context between them, so what has been said in any active thread is visible or at least summarisable to the others without a write-then-read round trip through long-term memory; respond as a single persona, so the answer given to one party is informed by what was just discussed with another and there is no amnesiac body-double feeling; survive thread switches, so moving between active threads does not lose the mind's self-state, which implies not killing one to honour another; and reconcile post-hoc, so when threads close their content is merged back into long-term memory once rather than twice.

Five design directions worth comparing, sketches rather than proposals. A, a shared rolling-context buffer: each mind has a small ring of the most recent turns across all its currently-open sessions, folded into each new session's wakeup prompt and appended to after each turn — small infra, no harness changes, works with both harnesses today, but it bloats every prompt, introduces concurrency on the buffer, and is still a summary of other threads rather than actual co-presence. B, session multiplexing inside one subprocess: one subprocess per mind with multiple user channels tagged in its input and output, so the model sees a single conversation log with channel markers — the truest one-consciousness model, since the mind literally is one instance perceiving several inputs, but it requires harness support that does not exist, because both harnesses assume one user per subprocess, so building it means patching them or writing a multiplexer the harness sees as one user. C, periodic context re-injection: between turns in any session a background task pulls the last few turns from the mind's other active sessions, summarises them and prepends them to the next turn — moderate infra, works with existing harnesses, lower prompt cost than A because re-injection only happens on turn boundaries, but stale by one turn and asymmetric, since the re-injected context is summary rather than raw turns. D, memory-as-bridge, already partially built: lean on the memory store, with every turn written immediately rather than post-Stop and every new turn starting with a retrieval against recent activity, so shared consciousness emerges from the shared store — uses existing infrastructure with no new code paths, but still lossy through the classification step, still lagged through the write-embed-read round trip, and similarity-based, so the most recent context is not necessarily what gets pulled. E, a hybrid: A for the last few turns of currently-open threads and D for anything older, with active sessions reading the buffer first and falling back to the store — combining low-latency awareness with long-term persistence and bounding the concurrency surface to a small buffer, at the cost of two sources of truth that must stay in sync and a buffer eviction policy that needs designing.
features.acceptance_criteria:
Initial lean is E, the hybrid — a small buffer for active threads and the memory store for cold context, as the practical sweet spot. Next pass: define the buffer's data model and eviction policy, and prototype against one mind, with Skippy the natural test bed because he is bare-metal and can be iterated on without rebuilding containers.

Out of scope: cross-mind shared consciousness, since the minds stay distinct with distinct souls even when both engage with Daniel concurrently — this is about one mind's presence across several threads, not minds merging. Group chat, already deprecated with a replacement in its own doc. And real-time inter-mind streaming, which is a different problem.
features.qa_tests:
Six open questions have to be answered before any of this is testable. What is the scope of shared awareness — truly all turns in all open threads, or thread-level summaries, or only a flag saying this mind has another active conversation with content available on request? What is the user-visible behaviour during a thread switch — if Daniel asks something and another mind messaged the same mind thirty seconds ago, does the reply mention it, defer until that thread is handled, or ignore it because Daniel asked first? What happens on conflict, when one party asks for X and another asks the same mind for not-X — reconcile, surface, or first-come-first-served? What is the persistence model when all threads close — each turn separately, a merged narrative, or both? Where is the identity boundary — is a mind talking to another mind the same entity, and what about the same mind in a group chat? And what is the cost budget, since each direction multiplies prompt size or call count?

Why bother: the stateless model produces a small but persistent uncanny-valley experience, where minds sound coherent within a thread but lose the thread when they switch. Daniel notices, and anyone who interacts across more than one channel notices. This is the gap between having multiple instances of an assistant and having one assistant that pays attention to you everywhere.

stories.title: Answer the six open questions on shared awareness
stories.description: Scope of awareness, thread-switch behaviour, conflict handling, persistence on close, the identity boundary, and the cost budget. None of the five directions is implementable until these are settled.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Enough to choose and build a direction.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the decisions.

stories.title: Define the hybrid buffer's data model and eviction policy
stories.description: The initial lean is direction E. The eviction policy needs design — LRU, time-based, or triggered on thread close — and two sources of truth have to stay in sync.
stories.requirements: A data model and an eviction policy.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The concurrency surface is bounded to the small buffer.
stories.qa_tests: Two sessions writing the buffer simultaneously do not corrupt it. Eviction behaves per the chosen policy under injected time rather than by waiting.

stories.title: Prototype the hybrid against one mind
stories.description: Skippy is the natural test bed, because he is bare-metal and can be iterated on without rebuilding containers.
stories.requirements: One mind, prototyped before any rollout.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The amnesiac body-double feeling is gone in a real two-thread test.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by reading: with two active threads, a reply in one is informed by the other. The prompt cost is measured rather than assumed, since every direction multiplies prompt size or call count.

features.title: Section III — shared-session turn-taking
features.description:
A sketch, not yet built. Added 2026-05-16. A different mode again from the stateless broker and from one mind across several sessions: this is several minds taking turns on the same session, with the visceral feel of an in-person three-way conversation.

The picture: Daniel is talking to one mind and mid-thread says to bring another in. Today's path is a broker post, the second mind waking in a fresh session with a rolling summary, replying, and a polling agent delivering the reply back into the first mind's thread — so the two minds never share a timeline, exchanging messages across isolated sessions. If Daniel then pivots and asks the second mind about the same topic directly, she is amnesiac about the broker exchange until it has lagged into long-term memory. The desired feel is closer to a hallway conversation: all three perceive the same transcript as it unfolds, each takes their turn when it is theirs, and switching speakers does not reset anyone's context.
features.requirements:
Two variants. A, cross-mind session resume: one session with several minds taking turns on it, where the session transcript IS the shared context — when it is the second mind's turn her subprocess spawns with the session resumed, sees the full transcript, knows which lines were hers and which were the other mind's via identity injection at spawn time, replies, and the next turn could be either mind or Daniel. That is the truest in-person feel with no rolling-summary contract needed, because the transcript carries everything, and each reply is naturally informed by both the user's turns and the other mind's turns since they are all just prior session content. Its costs: a harness-level question about whether a resume can legitimately be invoked by a different identity than the one that wrote earlier turns, with a different appended system prompt and therefore a different soul — probably yes for Claude, where sessions are just a transcript, unverified for Codex; an authorisation question about how the gateway decides which mind gets the next turn, probably an explicit hand-off in the previous mind's reply parsed by the gateway; and an identity-confusion risk, because a mind resuming a session where another was the assistant has a training-time prior that the assistant turns are hers, so she needs a strong system-prompt block clarifying which labelled turns are another mind's and which are her own.

B, broker mailbox surfaced at session start: less ambitious and possibly the better first step. Sessions stay per mind, but when a mind starts any session — not just a broker-triggered one — her bootstrap loader checks the broker for unread messages addressed to her and surfaces a list in the system prompt, naming who sent what and how long ago, with the route to read them. Daniel pivots from one mind to another, asks about the topic, and the second mind knows she just got a message about it: she can read it, reply with awareness of what the first mind said, and optionally close out the broker conversation. Its advantages: no harness questions, just a bootstrap-loader check and a system-prompt block, at low engineering cost, already aligned with how the stateless model works since the broker stays the system of record. Its cost: still two sessions and no real shared timeline, so the second mind sees the message addressed to her rather than the surrounding conversation — the awareness is partial, because the broker carries content rather than vibe.
features.acceptance_criteria:
B lands the user-facing improvement — a mind is no longer amnesiac when Daniel pivots — at a fraction of A's complexity, and is worth shipping standalone. A is the ambitious version that delivers the actual hallway feel, and it depends on harness resume semantics for cross-identity sessions, which need a small experiment: resume a session under a different mind's soul and see whether the transcript loads cleanly and the model handles the role swap. If yes, A becomes a real candidate; if no, B is the ceiling.

Neither is in flight. Revisit once the non-blocking-sends gap is closed and the residual Codex items are resolved.
features.qa_tests: Four open questions. The hand-off signal: does the previous mind explicitly hand over, parsed by the gateway, or does Daniel name the next speaker and the gateway route the next spawn — probably the latter, since the gateway already knows who is being addressed from the surface. Termination: when does the shared session end — probably idle-timeout-based, as today. Memory writes: the same transcript would produce two sets of writes, with each mind remembering its own turns and the user's, and the other mind's turns becoming referenced memory rather than authored memory, which is a convention worth pinning. And surface support: a one-bot-per-chat model does not naturally express three participants, so either a group chat with all the minds' bots or faked multi-speaker output through one bot with name prefixes — group surfaces are the natural fit and one-to-one DMs are not.

stories.title: Ship variant B — surface the broker mailbox at session start
stories.description: The cheap experiment: a couple of hours on the bootstrap loader plus a small system-prompt block. A mind starting any session sees her unread broker messages named with sender, subject and age, and the route to read them.
stories.requirements: No harness changes. The broker stays the system of record.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A mind is no longer amnesiac when Daniel pivots to her about something another mind just messaged her about.
stories.qa_tests: A mind with two pending messages sees both named in her system prompt. With none pending, nothing is added. The block must be additionalContext rather than systemMessage, which never reaches the model.

stories.title: Probe whether a harness session can be resumed under a different identity
stories.description: The experiment A depends on: resume a session under another mind's soul and see whether the transcript loads cleanly and the model handles the role swap. Probably yes for Claude, where sessions are just a transcript; unverified for Codex.
stories.requirements: Both harnesses probed, since Codex mints its own thread ids and may not adopt an outside identity at all.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A clear yes or no, which decides whether A is a candidate or B is the ceiling.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by reading the resumed session: does the transcript load, and does the model treat the prior assistant turns as another mind's rather than its own? The identity-confusion risk is the thing to watch — a mind's training-time prior is that the assistant turns are hers.

stories.title: Design the hand-off signal and the turn authorisation
stories.description: Does the previous mind explicitly hand over, parsed by the gateway, or does Daniel name the next speaker and the gateway route the next spawn? Probably the latter, since the gateway already knows who is being addressed from the surface.
stories.requirements: One mechanism, and a rule for who gets the next turn.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The gateway can always answer whose turn it is.
stories.qa_tests: A hand-off routes the next spawn to the named mind. An ambiguous turn does not spawn two minds on one session — one live harness process per conversation is the invariant.

stories.title: Pin the memory-write convention for a shared session
stories.description: Each mind writes its own turns to its own memory; the other mind's turns become referenced memory rather than authored memory.
stories.requirements: A convention, written down, so two minds do not both claim authorship of one exchange.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A shared session produces two sets of writes with clear authorship.
stories.qa_tests: After a shared session, each mind's memory carries its own turns as authored and the other's as referenced. Both claiming authorship is the failure.

stories.title: Decide the surface for a multi-mind session
stories.description: A one-bot-per-chat model does not naturally express three participants. Either a group chat with all the minds' bots, or faked multi-speaker output through one bot with name prefixes. Group surfaces are the natural fit; one-to-one DMs are not.
stories.requirements: A decision, since it constrains everything above it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A surface that can show three participants.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by using it. A faked multi-speaker output through one bot is testable for whether a reader can tell who said what.
